function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

Below is a **complete “recipe”** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, show the exact shell commands you’d run, and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow.  

> ⚠️ **Important** – I don’t have access to your machine or the remote repo, so I can’t actually *clone* or *push* anything for you.  
> The commands below assume you’re running them locally on a machine that already has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and the GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed, and that you’ve authenticated with GitHub via SSH (`ssh-agent` + key) or HTTPS+token.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have an SSH key added to your GitHub account
# (you can check with: ssh -T git@github.com)

git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the predominant language

> In practice you might want to run a script that counts lines per language, but here’s a quick one‑liner using `linguist` (the tool GitHub uses internally):

```bash
# Install linguist if you haven’t already
gem install github-linguist

# Get the dominant language
dominant=$(linguist --json | jq -r '.languages | max_by(.percent) | .name')
echo "Dominant language: $dominant"
```

> For this repo the output will be something like `JavaScript`.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

> **Using the helper function** (if you had a Python environment with the `create_a_docker_file` function available):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    port=3000,
    commands="npm ci; npm run build"
)
```

> **Or just write it yourself** – here’s a minimal Dockerfile that matches a typical Node.js app:

```Dockerfile
# File: nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build   # optional, only if you have a build step

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist   # adjust if your build outputs elsewhere
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]          # adjust entry point accordingly
```

> Save that file in the repo root.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

> Using the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome/k8s",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deploy",
    image_name="your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    service_type="ClusterIP",
    port=80,
    target_port=3000
)
```

> Or manually create two files:

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Adjust `image:` to point at whatever registry you’ll push to (e.g., Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, GCR, etc.).

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> • Add two repository secrets in GitHub Settings → Secrets → Actions:  
>   - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>   - `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token with `write:packages` scope  
> • If you’re using GitHub Packages instead, replace the login action with `docker/login-action@v3` using `registry: ghcr.io` and the appropriate secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/updated files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

> If you generated the files programmatically, they’ll already exist in the working tree; otherwise, make sure the paths match what you created above.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After the push, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow defined in `.github/workflows/build.yml`.  
> You can monitor the build status on the **Actions** tab of the repo.

---

## Quick sanity checks

| Check | Command |
|-------|---------|
| Verify Dockerfile builds locally | `docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .` |
| Run the image locally | `docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome` |
| Apply K8s manifests (assuming you have a cluster) | `kubectl apply -f k8s/` |
| Inspect the deployed pods | `kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome` |

---

### TL;DR – One‑liner cheat sheet

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git && cd nodejs-welcome
# (Generate Dockerfile, k8s YAMLs, and GitHub Actions file as shown above)
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once the push lands, the GitHub Actions workflow will build the image, push it to Docker Hub, and you’ll have everything ready for deployment. Happy coding!
